catalog_quote: The Tokyo dialect of Japanese exhibits lexical contrasts based on pitch accent; that is, there are minimal pairs of words that are identical segment-wise, but can be distinguished in terms of their pitch contours ... Phonetically speaking, an accented vowel is assigned a High tone followed by a Low tone on the following vowel, resulting in an abrupt H(igh)-L(ow) fall in F0, whereas unaccented words do not show such a fall. ... for words consisting of n-syllables, there are n+1 accent patterns ... a. i'noti+ga (initial accent) 'life+NOM' b. koko'ro+ga (penultimate accent) 'heart+NOM' c. atama'+ga (final accent) 'head+NOM' d. miyako+ga (unaccented) 'city+NOM' ... sweep_summary: Japanese (nucl1643) is in the catalog as 'tonal' (lexical pitch accent) on Kawahara 2015 (held). Of 66 works with stress in the title, about 30 concern word accent of Tokyo/standard Japanese; the rest are phrasal prosody, other dialects (Kyoto, Kagoshima, Tsuruoka, Koshikijima), proto-Japanese reconstruction, or noise (L2 English accents, rakugo rhythm, palatal 'prosody'). Newly downloaded and read (all with record): McCawley 1965 MIT thesis (open on MIT DSpace), Shimabukuro 2002 UH dissertation (ScholarSpace), Poppe 2015 UTokyo dissertation, Kubozono 2006 Lingua (Kobe repository accepted MS), Ding 2006 (JUL open access), Kibe 2010 (NINJAL repository, Japanese), Ito & Mester 2007/2013/2019 (author copies), Seo et al. 2019 (ICPhS), plus an extra open find not in the list, Weitzman 1970 (USC/ONR instrumental study, ERIC). Every one describes Tokyo Japanese as a pitch accent system: at most one HL fall per word/phrase, lexically present-or-absent and lexically located (n+1 patterns), antepenultimate default in loanwords, F0 not intensity the correlate, no word stress. None contradicts or refines the classification beyond what the held Kawahara 2015 already states; the McCawley 1965 statement is the best new first-hand corroboration but does not supersede Kawahara 2015. Unread items that would deepen but not change the record: Kubozono 2011 (Blackwell), 2012 (Lingua), 2008 (Oxford Handbook) - all paywalled, medium priority; the remaining paywalled/print items (Haraguchi 1988, Nishiyama 2010, Oshima 2014, compound-accent papers, Yoshida 1995 thesis, Bostrom 1993, Kubozono 1993, Akinaga 1985) are low. discovery relied on Crossref, CiNii, Semantic Scholar, DSpace/WEKO APIs and archive.org (OpenAlex and Bing were unusable).

new_statements.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched.

It never describes the accent system, but it treats Japanese word accent as a pitch pattern (H on one mora, L on the next) that varies lexically, which is consistent with the catalog's pitch accent (tonal) coding and with McCawley 1965. new_statements.rule_in_words: Only an incidental presupposition, not a description of the system: Japanese words carry lexical 'accent patterns' realised as pitch (high on one mora, low on the next), and the HL pattern with a high-pitched first syllable and low second is a common pattern across Sino-Japanese and Foreign vocabulary strata. new_statements.quote: In sum, the tone pattern of a Tokyo dialect word is described by two parameters: the presence or absence of an initial low mora, and the presence or absence of a fall from high to low. Moreover, the presence of the initial low mora is predictable. The initial mora is high if the first syllable is heavy or if the following mora is low; otherwise, the initial mora is low. The distinctive property of words is, then, the presence and location of the fall from high to low. [p.29] ... Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. [p.42]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tokyo Japanese has lexical pitch accent: the only distinctive word property is whether and where a high-to-low fall occurs; the initial low mora is predictable (first mora low unless the first syllable is heavy or the second mora is low). The tone-bearing unit is the mora but the accent domain is the syllable (in a heavy syllable the fall can only follow its first mora, p.35). No stress independent of pitch accent is normally recognised.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §1.5 (pp.42-49) discusses a possible non-contrastive 'stress system of sorts': a subjective impression of initial prominence on words (Hattori and Poser's consultants), phrase-final lengthening, and an alternating rhythm of bimoraic feet built left to right with the first mora of each foot stronger, whose 'principal if not only phonetic exponent is found in duration, not F0 or vowel quality' (p.43); Poser states no instrumental investigation had been made.
new_statements.exceptions: Words may be unaccented (no fall). Poser explicitly argues (p.42) that Hattori's prosodeme does not attribute non-tonal correlates to the accent itself.
new_statements.identity_note: Poser describes the Tokyo dialect (standard Japanese), as does the existing McCawley 1965 statement; Fon's Japanese subjects were Tokyo Japanese speakers from Tokyo and three neighbouring prefectures. No other variety is described in the opened works.

new_statements.quote: Japanese is not usually described as exhibiting any sort of stress independent of the pitch accent system. There is nonetheless some reason to believe that Tokyo dialect Japanese has a stress system of sorts. I have already cited Hattori's report that he has the impression of initial stress on words, and other speakers whom I have consulted confirm this subjective impression. Unfortunately, no instrumental investigation of this point has been carried out. In a similar vein, there is some evidence for phrase-final lengthening in Japanese. This suggests that there may be a word-level pattern of increased duration at the end and "stress" at the beginning.

new_statements.quote: Theoretically, a lexical accent may land on any one of the vowels in a word. However, in Standard Japanese, if a word consists of three 'syllables (in traditional terms)' or less, the lexical accent location is random, unlike longer words whose accent location is predictable (Haraguchi 1991). Also, it is said that there is class of nouns without lexical accent. [...] Note that the pitch pattern is predictable if the location of the accent is known. [...] accent location in certain classes of words is predictable, and accordingly Standard Japanese should be regarded as any other stress system: to wit, the stress (accent) location is predictable, if it is not specified lexically.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (lexical pitch accent in Tokyo/Standard Japanese: presence vs absence and location of one accent, pitch contour predictable from it), so no contradiction; adds placement detail not in the Kawahara record or the McCawley/Poser statements: accent location is lexically free only in short nouns (<=3 OR pairs/moras: n+1 classes incl. unaccented), long morphologically simplex nouns and loanwords take default antepenultimate accent, short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless, the domain-initial nucleus is never high unless itself accented, and compound/verb/phrase accent is derived by the same principles; Yoshida treats the system formally as a stress system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Standard (Tokyo) Japanese is a lexical pitch accent language: a word has at most one accent (or none); from the accented nucleus leftwards all nuclei except the word-initial one are high, nothing after it is high, so the contour follows from the accent location. In nouns of up to three moras (OR pairs) the accent location (or its absence) is lexical (n+1 classes: na'mida, tama'go, takara', kuruma); morphologically simplex nouns of four or more OR pairs and long loanwords get default antepenultimate accent (mura'saki, hototo'gisu, suto'resu, puro'guramu), analysed as the head of the penultimate right-headed foot; short lexically unmarked nouns surface accentless; compound, noun+particle, verb and sentence accent are derived from the members' lexical properties by the same licensing principles. The author argues the formalism is identical to stress assignment (predictable unless lexically specified).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None posited: only one head (accent) per domain; footnote 6 p.78 says only primary prominence is discussed. No stress independent of pitch accent is claimed anywhere in the thesis.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically marked short nouns and some loans keep accent off the default site; final-accented and accentless nouns are homophonous in isolation and distinguished only before particles (-ga); 'devoiced' high vowels and the moraic nasal cannot bear accent, shifting it (sec. 3.3); genitive -no deaccents certain final-accented nouns (sec. 4.3.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Yoshida 1995 treats Standard (Tokyo) Japanese; Bostrom 1993 (title) treats Japanese pitch accent generally, presumably Tokyo standard; Otaka 2009 treats standard Japanese rhythm/timing (moras, feet, geminates); Hirata 2006 is Japanese syntax.

tone_statements.citation: Urasoko, Rie. 2023. De-Accentuation in Tokyo Japanese. Radical: A Journal of Phonology, 168-202.
tone_statements.quote: The prominence of a pitch accent is determined by the difference in pitch height. The distinctive lexical pitch accent is marked phonetically by the sequence from high pitched mora (henceforth H) to low pitched mora (henceforth L). This accent is located on the last H pitched mora immediately before the tonal dropping towards L pitched mora, which is called “accent kernel”. Thus, only the tonal fall (HL) marks a placement of lexical accent (if there is one). ... The Japanese lexicon is divided into two accentual patterns: accented and unaccented. ... The accent kernel can be located on any mora.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 169-170, sec. 1.1 'Accent in Tokyo Japanese' (footnote number 1 after 'accent kernel' elided)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo-type pitch accent: words accented (one HL fall, kernel on any mora) or unaccented; H/L are mora pitch heights, no tone count; at least 22 accent-marked forms pp. 170-172.

tone_statements.citation: Urasoko, Rie. 2023. Le patron atone et le phénomène de la désaccentuation en japonais moderne [The atonic pattern and the deaccentuation phenomenon in contemporary Japanese]. Thèse de doctorat, Université Bordeaux Montaigne (dir. Laurence Labrune). NNT 2023BOR30057.
tone_statements.quote: Le japonais est communément catégorisé comme une langue à accent de hauteur ... L’accent lexical du japonais se révèle donc dans la différence de niveau de hauteur mélodique. Il existe en principe deux hauteurs distinctives, haut (désormais H) et bas (B) et le noyau accentuel se situe immédiatement devant la descente tonale. ... contrairement à l’analyse de Poser (1984), ainsi qu’à notre propre analyse basée sur un système à ton H privatif dans lequel B est phonologiquement inactif. ... Nous considérons ainsi, pour notre part, que les éléments que nous avons mis au jour pointent fortement en faveur d’une analyse tonale, au sens plein, du japonais de Tōkyō.
tone_statements.translation: Japanese is commonly categorised as a pitch-accent language ... The lexical accent of Japanese thus shows itself in the difference of melodic pitch level. There are in principle two distinctive pitches, high (henceforth H) and low (B), and the accent kernel is located immediately before the tonal fall. ... contrary to Poser's (1984) analysis, as well as to our own analysis based on a privative H-tone system in which B (low) is phonologically inactive. ... We thus consider, for our part, that the elements we have brought to light point strongly in favour of a tonal analysis, in the full sense, of Tokyo Japanese.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 74-75, §2.3 sub-section 'Accent lexical de hauteur du japonais: noyau accentuel et niveaux de hauteur'; then p. 520 and p. 523, §7.3 'Le japonais de Tōkyō est-il une langue à tons ?'

tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese described as pitch accent (H/B, accent kernel before the fall, tonic vs atonic words, mora as accent unit), then reanalysed as privative H-vs-zero tone with floating H, surface H/M/B.

tone_statements.citation: Ito, Junko & Mester, Armin (2019). Pitch accent and tonal alignment in Kagoshima Japanese. The Linguistic Review 36: 1-24.
tone_statements.quote: ...the dialects of Kagoshima Japanese have only two patterns, regardless of the length of the word (“N-pattern systems”). The first is the HL pattern (also called “Type A”), which aligns a H(igh) L(ow) sequence with the end of the word, preceded by a sequence of L-toned syllables. The second is the H pattern (also called “Type B”) which consists in a final H tone, also preceded by L-toned syllables. ... For our purposes here, we follow the tonal analysis of Kubozono (2012) and simply take the two tonal melodies as lexically given.

tone_statements.summary: Two-pattern (N-pattern) pitch accent: lexical melodies HL (Type A) vs H (Type B) aligned to the word end, syllable by syllable in Kagoshima City; data from Kubozono.

tone_statements.citation: Kubozono, Haruo. 2017. Accent in Japanese phonology. In Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics. New York: Oxford University Press.
tone_statements.quote: Japanese dialects have pitch accent systems, systems where pitch, rather than intensity or other phonetic features, is used as the primary phonetic property of words (Beckman, 1986 ). Moreover, most dialects, including Tokyo Japanese, use pitch contrastively ... Most of them are sensitive to an abrupt pitch fall and use it as the primary phonetic correlate of the phonological pitch accent (Hattori, 1960 ; McCawley, 1968 ; Pierrehumbert & Beckman, 1988 ). This can be demonstrated by the following data from Tokyo Japanese, where lexical meanings can be differentiated by the presence or absence of a pitch fall as well as the position of the pitch fall.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese lexical pitch accent: words accented (place of an abrupt pitch fall) or unaccented; (n+1) patterns for n-syllable nouns; no H/L tone inventory; downstep named as a phrasal process.

tone_statements.citation: Ito, Junko & Mester, Armin. 2016. Unaccentedness in Japanese. Linguistic Inquiry 47(3): 471-526. doi:10.1162/ling_a_00219
tone_statements.quote: The phonetic characteristics of Japanese pitch contours ... include two main features, the initial rise and the accentual fall. The pitch contour of a prosodic word—more precisely, of a minor phrase ...—begins with a boundary %Low and then proceeds on a phrasal High until it reaches the accented syllable, if present. The accentual High*Low complex is a steep fall, as on the syllable ra in a form like tabesaseráreta ‘was made to eat’. In the absence of an accent, as in iresaserareta ‘was made to insert’, the pitch stays on the phrasal High. The concatenation of these tones results in the overall pattern %Low+High+(High*Low)%.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Tokyo Japanese lexical pitch accent: the accented syllable carries a High*Low fall, docked on its head mora (p. 489, fn. 14); unaccented words stay on phrasal High.

tone_statements.citation: Labrune, Laurence. 2013. Le japonais. Lalies (Langues et littérature: actes des sessions de linguistique et de littérature) 33: 171-219.
tone_statements.quote: Le japonais de Tokyo est connu pour son accent de hauteur ... Les mots japonais appartiennent à la classe accentuée ou inaccentuée. Les mots accentués possèdent une more qui constitue le noyau accentuel du mot, après laquelle se produit une chute tonale. C'est donc le passage d'une tonalité haute à une tonalité basse qui marque la position de l'accent au niveau du mot. Les mots inaccentués ne possèdent pas de passage de haut à bas. ... a) il n'y a qu'un seul passage de haut à bas dans un mot accentué ... b) les deux mores initiales du mot doivent être de tonalité différente, soit haut - bas, soit bas – haut.
tone_statements.translation: Tokyo Japanese is known for its pitch accent ... Japanese words belong to the accented or the unaccented class. Accented words have a mora that constitutes the accent nucleus of the word, after which a tonal fall occurs. It is thus the transition from a high pitch to a low pitch that marks the position of the accent at word level. Unaccented words have no high-to-low transition. ... a) there is only one high-to-low transition in an accented word ... b) the first two morae of the word must differ in pitch, either high-low or low-high.
tone_statements.locator: section 2.5 L'accent (no page numbers; published version pp. 171-219)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source

sources.quote: A sentence of standard Japanese is divided into phonological phrases (bunsetsu) each of which may contain at most one significant fall in pitch. I will refer to the syllable or mora where this fall in pitch occurs as the accented mora or syllable of the phrase. Then, disregarding intonational factors, the morae of a phonological phrase display the following pitches: the morae up to and including the accented mora are high-pitched, except that the first mora is low-pitched if it is not accented; the morae after the accented mora are low-pitched; in phonological phrases which contain no accented mora, the first mora is low-pitched and all subsequent morae high-pitched.

sources.quote: Japanese words may be either accented, in which case they carry a single pitch accent (henceforth accent), or unaccented. sources.quote: The phonetic characteristics of Japanese pitch contours ... include two main features, the initial rise and the accentual fall. The pitch contour of a prosodic word—more precisely, of a minor phrase ...—begins with a boundary %Low and then proceeds on a phrasal High until it reaches the accented syllable, if present. The accentual High*Low complex is a steep fall, as on the syllable ra in a form like tabesaseráreta ‘was made to eat’. In the absence of an accent, as in iresaserareta ‘was made to insert’, the pitch stays on the phrasal High. The concatenation of these tones results in the overall pattern %Low+High+(High*Low)%.

tone.translation: As explained before (this journal no. 49, p. 63), the most rational way to mark accent is to use the three signs (⏋)(—)(⎿) corresponding to the three levels upper, middle, lower. ... As I have said repeatedly, this is a notation of pitch accent and has nothing to do with stress accent. ... ⎿a⏋ozo⏋ra 'blue sky', ⎿ka⏋raka⏋sa 'umbrella', ⎿ko⏋mamono⏋ya 'haberdasher' ...
